Appendix B • Proofs & Comments

B.9 Connections and covariant derivatives (§6.1)

In Chapter 6 the words connection and covariant derivative are used almost interchangeably: the connection is the structure \(\nabla\), and the covariant derivative is what it produces, \(\nabla_\mathcal{X} T\). In differential geometry at large, however, the two notions are genuinely different, the connection being the more general one. This appendix sketches the difference.

  • Connections live on any bundle. Consider a smooth bundle \(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\), with arbitrary fibres. At each point \(e\) of the total space, the tangent space \(T_eE\) contains a canonical vertical subspace, \(V_eE \coloneqq \ker (d\pi)_e\), made of the directions along the fibre, which the projection collapses to zero. There is, however, no canonical notion of horizontal direction, i.e. of moving along \(\mathcal{M}\) without moving within the fibre. A (Ehresmann) connection is precisely such a choice: a smooth assignment of horizontal subspaces \(H_eE\) complementary to the vertical ones, \[ T_eE = V_eE \oplus H_eE . \] From it one obtains parallel transport: a curve in \(\mathcal{M}\) can be lifted uniquely to a horizontal curve in \(E\) through any chosen point of the initial fibre. Nothing in this construction requires the fibres to be vector spaces. On a principal \(G\)-bundle one additionally demands compatibility with the action of \(G\), and the connection can be equivalently encoded as a Lie-algebra-valued 1-form.

  • Covariant derivatives live on vector bundles. A covariant derivative is a linear differential operator acting on sections of a vector bundle \(E \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathcal{M}\), \[ \nabla : \Gamma T\mathcal{M} \times \Gamma E \longrightarrow \Gamma E, \] \(C^\infty(\mathcal{M})\)-linear in its first argument and satisfying the product rule \(\nabla_\mathcal{X}(g\,s) = \mathcal{X}\left\lfloor g \right\rceil s + g \, \nabla_\mathcal{X} s\) in its second one. Both properties require adding sections and multiplying them by scalar fields, which only makes sense when the fibres are vector spaces.

  • Where they meet. On a vector bundle, the connections whose horizontal subspaces are compatible with the linear structure of the fibres (linear connections) are in one-to-one correspondence with covariant derivatives: \(\nabla_\mathcal{X} s\) is the vertical part of the derivative of the section \(s\) along \(\mathcal{X}\), the vertical subspaces of a vector bundle being canonically identified with the fibres themselves. A connection is therefore more general in two ways: it exists on bundles where covariant derivatives cannot even be defined, most notably principal bundles, and even on vector bundles there are non-linear connections that yield no covariant derivative.

  • A physics example. In gauge theories the gauge potential \(A\) is a connection on a principal \(G\)-bundle, not a derivative of anything. The familiar covariant derivative \(D_j = \partial_j - i A_j\) only appears when \(A\) acts on matter fields, which are sections of associated vector bundles.

In general relativity all the relevant objects are sections of the tangent bundle and of the tensor bundles built from it, which are vector bundles. There the two notions coincide, and the connection can be defined directly through the axioms of a covariant derivative, as done in Chapter 6.
